_about: Major energy outlooks and pathways, compared on common 2050 metrics. Values come from each publisher's own public summaries (latest edition available). '~' marks approximate or derived values; null means the publisher does not report it publicly. Political achievability and likelihood are editorial judgements (Claude's suggested starting point), not data. Your own likelihood score is stored on your device. Edit this file to add scenarios or correct values.

today.label: Today (2024–25)
today.note: Approximate current values: fossil share of primary energy ~79–80% (IEA), electricity ~21% of final energy (IEA WEO 2025), renewables ~32% of power, ~377 GW nuclear operable (IAEA PRIS), oil ~104 mb/d, total energy investment ~USD 3.3 trillion/yr (IEA World Energy Investment 2025).

metrics.label: Warming by 2100
metrics.desc: Global temperature rise above pre-industrial in 2100, as stated by the publisher (median or 50% unless noted). Publishers that don't estimate it show 'not published'.

metrics.label: Energy CO₂ in 2050 vs today
metrics.desc: Change in energy-related CO₂ emissions by 2050 relative to the base year of the outlook (2023–2025; IPCC uses 2019 and net CO₂).

metrics.label: Net-zero CO₂ year
metrics.desc: Year global (energy) CO₂ emissions reach net zero, where the outlook says so.

metrics.label: Fossil share of primary energy, 2050
metrics.desc: Coal + oil + natural gas as a share of total primary energy supply in 2050. Today ~80%.

metrics.label: Renewables share of electricity, 2050
metrics.desc: Share of electricity generation from renewables (solar, wind, hydro, bioenergy, geothermal) in 2050. Today ~32%.

metrics.label: Nuclear capacity, 2050
metrics.desc: Installed nuclear capacity in 2050. Today ~377 GW.

metrics.label: Oil demand, 2050
metrics.desc: Global oil demand in 2050, million barrels per day. Today ~104 mb/d.

metrics.label: Electricity share of final energy, 2050
metrics.desc: How much of the energy end users consume (buildings, industry, transport) arrives as electricity. Today ~21%. The main measure of electrification.

metrics.label: Electricity demand growth to 2050
metrics.desc: Growth in electricity demand (or generation) from the base year to 2050.

metrics.label: Total energy demand 2050 vs today
metrics.desc: Change in total primary energy demand to 2050. Falling demand usually reflects efficiency and electrification, not less energy service.

metrics.label: Energy investment, 2030s
metrics.desc: Annual energy-sector investment the pathway implies, around 2030–2035. Today ~USD 3.3 tn/yr. Scope differs between publishers (total vs clean-only), so compare with care.

scenarios.name: IEA Current Policies (CPS)
scenarios.summary: Only policies already in force; no new ones. Brought back in 2025 after US policy shifts. Oil and gas demand keep growing to 2050 and emissions plateau near today's level.

co2.note: stays close to 2024 level (~38 Gt) through 2050

invest.note: investment stays broadly flat at today's level to 2035

facts: Gas demand rises to 5,600 bcm by 2050

political.why: Needs no new policy at all: it is the 'do nothing more' baseline.

likelihood.why: A floor rather than a forecast. It freezes policy for 25 years, and ex-post studies show outlooks like this have consistently underestimated how fast solar, wind and batteries spread.

scenarios.name: IEA Stated Policies (STEPS)
scenarios.summary: Policies in force plus those governments have formally announced and are likely to implement. The most-cited 'central' view of where the world is heading.

co2.note: falls below 30 Gt by 2050 from ~38 Gt

mix.note: Fossil 21% and renewables ~two-thirds are stated; nuclear is the remainder.

facts: Coal and oil peak around 2030; gas plateaus mid-2030s

political.why: Already announced by governments, though some measures (e.g. in the US) have since been rolled back.

likelihood.why: The closest thing to a consensus central case. Watch for slippage on announced policy and upside on clean-tech deployment.

scenarios.name: IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE)
scenarios.summary: Works backwards from net-zero energy CO₂ by 2050. Electrification, efficiency, renewables (tripled by 2030) and a doubling of nuclear, with carbon removal later in the century.

invest.note: clean-energy investment by early 2030s (Net Zero Roadmap 2023)

facts: Relies on CO₂ removal to bring warming back down

political.why: Needs every major economy to act at once from now on. UNEP's 2025 Emissions Gap Report says the 1.5 °C limit will likely be breached within the decade.

likelihood.why: Useful as a benchmark of what 1.5 °C requires, not as a forecast.

scenarios.name: BNEF Economic Transition Scenario
scenarios.model: BNEF NEO model (least-cost, no new policy)
scenarios.summary: Technologies are deployed only where they're cheapest, with no new climate policy. Driven by falling solar, wind and battery costs.
facts: Solar becomes the largest power source of any kind by 2032
Gas overtakes oil as largest primary energy source by mid-2040s

political.why: Driven by economics, so it needs little new policy. It still needs permitting, grids and trade to keep working.

likelihood.why: Cost-driven and close to observed deployment trends. Its warming estimate is similar to IEA STEPS.

scenarios.name: BNEF Net Zero Scenario
scenarios.summary: A net-zero-by-2050 pathway with a ~500 GtCO₂ budget for 2024–2050. Heavier on renewables and storage, with large-scale carbon capture.

political.why: Investment would have to roughly triple within a decade.

likelihood.why: A normative benchmark. Note that it lands at ~1.7 °C, not 1.5 °C.

scenarios.name: DNV Energy Transition Outlook
scenarios.summary: A single 'most likely' forecast rather than a scenario set. Electrification and solar dominate; hydrogen and CCS scale more slowly and cost more than hoped.

mix.note: DNV reports the mix for 2060: solar 46%, wind 31%.

political.why: It is DNV's best guess of what will actually happen, including political friction.

likelihood.why: A best-estimate forecast with a good track record on renewables. It is more pessimistic on hydrogen and CCS than the IEA.

scenarios.name: ExxonMobil Global Outlook
scenarios.summary: ExxonMobil's projection: oil stays above 100 mb/d and gas grows ~20%. Emissions fall only ~17%, which the company says is ~3× the IPCC 'likely below 2 °C' level for 2050.
facts: Wind+solar rise from ~3% to >11% of primary energy

political.why: Assumes today's policy direction continues with modest tightening.

likelihood.why: Plausible on demand, but likely low on electrification and solar compared with recent trends. Read it with the publisher's interest in oil and gas in mind.

scenarios.name: OPEC World Oil Outlook (Reference)
scenarios.summary: Energy demand +23% to 2050, driven by India and other developing economies. Oil keeps a ~30% share, with no peak in sight.

invest.note: USD 17.7 tn upstream+downstream oil 2026–2050; total energy not stated

political.why: Needs only continued investment and policy inertia.

likelihood.why: The highest oil path of all outlooks here. It is the producers' view and ignores most of the EV and efficiency trends other outlooks include.

scenarios.name: bp Current Trajectory
scenarios.summary: Today's policies and technology trends continue. Energy security concerns slow the transition compared with earlier bp outlooks.

temp2100.note: bp: not consistent with Paris goals

facts: Coal ~15%, gas ~25%, renewables ~25% of primary energy in 2050

likelihood.why: Middle of the pack, close to IEA STEPS on emissions. bp itself says neither scenario is a forecast.

scenarios.name: bp Below 2°
scenarios.summary: Emissions cut ~90% by 2050, consistent with 'well below 2 °C'. Strong electrification, nuclear more than doubles, and gas with CCS.
facts: ~60% of remaining gas paired with CCS

political.why: Needs coordinated policy across major economies, but less extreme than 1.5 °C pathways.

likelihood.why: Plausible only with a policy step-change in the late 2020s.

scenarios.name: IRENA 1.5°C Scenario
scenarios.edition: World Energy Transitions Outlook 2024 (Nov 2024) — 2026 edition released Oct 2026
scenarios.summary: A renewables-led 1.5 °C pathway: tripled renewables by 2030, electricity over half of final energy, and green hydrogen for hard-to-abate sectors. Gives nuclear only a small role.

mix.note: Renewables 91%; the remaining 9% split between nuclear and gas/CCS is not detailed.

political.why: Same problem as all 1.5 °C pathways, plus heavy reliance on rapid grid build-out.

likelihood.why: Normative benchmark. Its high renewables share is a design choice, not a forecast.

scenarios.name: IPCC AR6 — C1 (1.5 °C, limited overshoot)
scenarios.model: Ensemble of integrated assessment models (MESSAGE, REMIND, IMAGE, GCAM, WITCH, …)
scenarios.summary: The median of 97 peer-reviewed model pathways that hold warming to 1.5 °C with no or limited overshoot. The scientific reference point, though now dated: emissions since 2019 have tracked well above it.

mix.note: Medians across all AR6 mitigation pathways: wind+solar 40–80%, nuclear ~10% (IQR 5–20%), CCS-equipped plants 5–10%.

political.why: Emissions have kept rising since 2019, so these pathways now need faster cuts than when published.

likelihood.why: Practically out of reach without a large overshoot and CO₂ removal (UNEP 2025).

scenarios.name: IPCC AR6 — C3 (likely below 2 °C)
scenarios.summary: The median of 311 pathways keeping warming likely (>67%) below 2 °C. Slower fossil phase-out, net-zero CO₂ in the 2070s.

political.why: UNEP 2025: full implementation of all net-zero pledges gives ~1.9 °C, so the political commitments exist on paper.

likelihood.why: Requires pledges to be fully delivered. Current policies point to ~2.8 °C.

scenarios.name: LUT 100% Renewable Energy
scenarios.model: LUT Energy System Transition Model (hourly, 145 regions)
scenarios.summary: A cost-optimised, fully renewable, sector-coupled global system by 2050, dominated by solar PV, with no nuclear or fossil fuels and no negative-emission technologies.

mix.note: Solar ~76% of total energy supply, wind ~20%.

facts: Energy cost similar to or below today

political.why: Requires phasing out all fossil and nuclear generation within 25 years worldwide.

likelihood.why: An important 'proof of possibility' that anchors the 100% RE side of the debate (see the Heard vs Brown papers in Studies).

scenarios.name: IAEA nuclear projection — Low case
scenarios.summary: Nuclear-only projection: conservative case assuming current trends continue. Useful to compare against the nuclear numbers in full-system scenarios.

political.why: Projects already under construction or firmly planned.

likelihood.why: Comparable to the IEA CPS nuclear figure (728 GW).

scenarios.name: IAEA nuclear projection — High case
scenarios.summary: Nuclear-only projection: the COP28 'tripling nuclear' ambition largely delivered, including SMRs. Close to the IEA NZE nuclear figure.

political.why: Strong political tailwinds (US, China, Japan, EU taxonomy, World Bank), but supply chains, financing and fuel (HALEU) are bottlenecks.

likelihood.why: History of construction delays and cost overruns argues for caution.
